title: Content Maxxing
content:
Lars Pinkwart is a researcher based in Zurich.

Down the rabbit hole:

The affix -maxxing denotes a form of radical optimization, the most known use of which is so called looksmaxxing, which describes various methods of self-optimisation: from facial gymnastics to practices such as bone-smashing or extensive plastic surgery, aimed at ascending to a higher position within the rigid social and aesthetic order of the manosphere. Since then, the affix has spread around social media, sometimes in earnest, oftentimes in transgressive ways: users document how they are sleepmaxxing, booksmaxxing, laughmaxxing, or even joymaxxing.

The phenomenon of -maxxing is indicative of a larger trend within digital cultures and specifically the way in which platforms have and continue to shape aesthetics and define standards of beauty, status and representation: the visual standards of looksmaxxing, just as much as its overall virality and circulation as a practice within certain groups of users, are contingent on social media and their platform economies. They in turn also stand in and visualise the specific logic of optimization already shaping digital visual cultures, and could offer an interpretative framework through which to analyse how generative AI and synthetic media -maxx these tendencies.

As synthetic media flood social media platforms, their reception from a critical audience has been largely negative, focusing on their kitsch aesthetics, highlighting visual flaws and analyzing them as mean or slop (Merriam-Webster’s 2025 word of the year) and overall emblematic of a degradation of culture, or even devoid of any particular style. What this analysis sometimes obfuscates however, is that within the framework of platform economies, this is actually supra-content which is high-performing, successful and highly optimised. This success is reflected in the strategies of companies like Meta, which, after initially aiming to disincentivise synthetic content on their platforms, seem to now go all in by building social feeds aimed exclusively at synthetic media, such as Meta’s Vibes or OpenAI’s Sora app. It is also the grounds for OpenAI‘s recent redirection of their business model, going all in on the platform economy and its media: short-form video, sexual and explicit content and social engagement (“usage-maxxing”) to “make some money” along the way to “AI that can do science”.

Ratings, Scores and Dump Stats

A particular fraction of looksmaxxers engage in knowledge exchange and ‘peer review’ on anonymous message boards. Evaluating someone else’s facial or body aesthetics has become a central practice on these boards, and the scores one receives in turn influence what is called one’s sexual market value. Through these evaluations and ratings, “discernible patterns within the community’s collective imagination, visual tapestry, and fantasies” are rendered visible. This process of evaluating aesthetics through user ratings on forums and boards in order to elicit shared patterns is also central to the creation of ‘aesthetics’ datasets in the training of generative AI models. LAION-Aesthetics V2, a subset of the LAION 5B dataset used to train both Stable Diffusion and Midjourney, incorporated the Aesthetic Visual Analysis (AVA) dataset, which was based on photos rated on the web forum dpchallenge, where users were rating each others photos from 1 to 10. Synthetic media, as Roland Meyer has argued extensively, is further defined by ‘platform realism’ as an aesthetics of competition, where media constantly compete with each other for attention, high rankings and interaction rates.

In accordance with the logic of -maxxing, synthetic media are stripped of ‘unnecessary’ parameters and focus solely on those parameters which guarantee high performance scores in the arena of the platform. After all, the affix itself supposedly references the gaming strategy of min-maxing, aimed at maximising the stats of a character which help the most at succeeding, while reducing those which do not immediately contribute to this specific goal, creating in turn characters which are highly optimised for a specific task but not well rounded and overall unrealistic. In these forms of instrumental play, a specific parameter – called the “dump stat” – is sometimes sacrificed, in order to distribute resources to those stats which one wants to maximize. Those players who began min-maxing are sometimes called ‘roll players’, rather than ‘role players’, to highlight how they reduced storytelling and the experience of playing to the mechanics of the game. -Maxxing, and its origins, are ultimately expressions of a specific logic of radical optimisation, which works both through the focus on and the exaggeration of a few parameters, and in turn the neglect of other parameters and overall ‘rounded-ness’.

Steering a Concept

A viral trend in the context of early generative image models began with the generation of a starting image prompted with a specific feature or concept, which the model was in turn prompted to exaggerate, to ‘make it more __’. The trend speculated on the question of what the most exaggerated form of this concept or parameter would look like. Essentially, the trend operationalised the specific way in which concepts of style and vibe guide image generation, in which, to stay in this visual sphere, muscles are not a relational part of the human anatomy but are defined by a latent concept of muscle-ness which can be continuously amplified.

In their project “xhairymutantx”(2024), Holly Herndon and Matt Dryhurst take on this logic of exaggeration, in an attempt of steering and hijacking the concept of Holly Herndon herself within the latent space of the model, an approach which they name ‘cliche poisoning’. After inspecting the training dataset of popular image models such as Stable Diffusion and finding images of herself within them, and by experimenting with these models and prompting them with her name, Herndon concludes that her concept is essentially defined by her signature red hair. Together with Dryhurst, she begins to construct a ‘golem’ character with exaggerated features and a distinct haircut and uses it to finetune an image model which is made available on the website of the Whitney museum. Through the generation of a large amount of variations, and as she states in the accompanying video essay – also through press on the protests critical of their work and the Whitney museum exhibition – she speculates on shifting the latent space of future models towards this exaggerated concept of herself. The politics of attention, which in the context of platforms already manifest themselves in strategies of gaming the algorithm, the production of controversy and the mobilisation of vibes, are transformed here, aiming instead at presence and dominance in the latent space, which is achieved through the focus and radical optimisation of a few parameters or characteristics, taking on the models reductive encoding and reinforcing it further.

Maxxing ones presence in the latent spaces of generative models binds what could be called cultural market value directly to what Mikael Brunila has analysed as ‘cosine capital’: the commodification of embeddings, learned by the model from the training data. Here, cultural capital is acquired not through the opinions of legacy media tastemakers or the attention of networked masses (although at least in Herndon & Dryhurst’s conception these are still useful), but through what Leonardo Impett and Fabian Offert call ‘neural exchange value’: through the ability to be easily represented as a vector – or in Herndon & Dryhurst terms, as a concept – and to effectively mobilise both the relational modality and the dimensionality reduction of vector spaces.

Content Farming and The Politics of Variability

Backed by a one million dollar cash injection from Marc Andreessen’s and Ben Horowitz’s venture capital firm a16z, the startup Doublespeed has pitched what is essentially a farming service for synthetic content. The introduction video for the company presents an ideological soup of gen-z lore, late stage capitalist grift and cultural nihilism: the internet is “already dead anyway”, you’ve been watching slop (aka ‘legacy media’) all your life, and bot farms shouldn’t be left to the Russia and China.

The startup is emblematic of a larger pool of young male college students or dropouts pitching controversial startups to stand out in the flood of AI grifts, such as the AI assistant Cluely ($20.3 million from a16z and others) aimed at “cheating on everything”, or the brainrot code editor and development environment called Chad IDE ($500,000 from Y Combinator), which bridges the short wait during inference in AI-assisted coding by showing you brainrot content, allowing you to ‘shit-post on X’ or ‘swipe Tinder’. What these examples show is a general trend within VC-funding which itself mobilises virality and controversy in the attempt to farm attention and in this case, literal capital. In a sense, Doublespeed, Cluely and ChadIDE represent the perfect blueprint of what a min-maxed startup would look like, one which has perhaps sacrificed a dump stat too many.

On their website, Doublespeed promises to ‘automate attention’ by generating ‘synthetic influencers’ with ‘hyper-specific personas’. These personas are effectively min-maxed, defined through only a few parameters or “consistent patterns” which shape their ‘background’: those parameters which allow the model to optimally target a particular niche of platform users. Essentially, all the parameters to which users have been reduced on platforms in the context of content recommendation systems, now return as the targets of optimised generation.

The aspect of farming further highlights a second central aspect of this logic of content maxxing: not only exaggeration, but also variability plays an important role. Doublespeed for example proposes to “take proven content and spawn variation”, with “each unique enough to avoid suppression”. Much like the variations of Holly Herndon’s golem, this represents an attempt which mobilises the farming of variation in order to project a strong concept. The individual image or video or text, if we follow Meta’s argument in a court on the copyright violations of its AI models, is after all not much more than noise, only able to steer the performance of the model by “less than 0.06 percent”. The strategy of variability aims at increasing this percentage while avoiding to trigger spam filters and be in turn suppressed by the algorithm. To farm variability based on a highly min-maxed, exaggerated and specific persona becomes necessary for the projection of a strong concept. After all, the agency within the ecology of platforms further shifts, as was argued last November in a discussion on ‘Post-AI Art’, from the production of singular works to either the design of systems able to generate and spawn variable content at scale, or the design of those systems underlying the feeds and models themselves.

Variability also holds, at least in Herndon and Dryhurst‘s conception, the potential that current outputs of generative models will become the training data for future models. As Brunila argues, generative models require a “closed environment of data that must be constantly replenished and expanded” in order to prevent collapse “towards the mean”. (Brunila, 2025) Trying to replenish the models environment with synthetic data which lacks outside contingency can lead to model collapse, which was framed by Jathan Sadowski as “Habsburg AI”, a system that is so extensively trained “on the outputs of other generative AI's that it becomes an inbred mutant”. Sadowski referenced the so-called ‘Habsburg Jaw’, which likely was a consequence of inbreeding within the ruling family.

In his works “Habsburg AI Portrait Studies”, Martin Disley tests out this theory by experimenting with recursively fine-tuning diffusion models on their own output. Disley not only aims to visualise this idea of modal collapse, but to also highlight the specific aesthetic style of – in this case MidjourneyV5,- and how ranking and user feedback is used to encode certain aesthetic preferences. This model style is less apparent in the stylised outputs directly from the model but becomes more apparent through recursion. Their redoubling in the recursive processes reveals a “min-maxed” aesthetic which is optimised towards performance in the tested context of the social feed, while minimising other parameters. While the initial outputs of generative models like Midjourney might appear to be ‘generic’, or devoid of any particular style or aesthetic, the recursion of training on synthetic data quickly reveals how min-maxed they really are.

Convergence

As content generation and social media increasingly merge, their modes of operation, and thus forms of valorisation, seem to be headed towards convergence. As much as users on social media already optimize their own content for the algorithm, the recursive process between the generation and consumption of synthetic content will only -maxx these tendencies further. The fantasy of the “make it more __” trend, to search for the most exaggerated form of a concept, is thus revealing a general tendency towards an ‘instrumental convergence’ of popular culture, as the model, and in turn its users, optimise towards high-performing, and thus highly exaggerated and variable content.

If these are the modalities within which we operate on platforms, then cultural market value is defined by taking part in the game of what Herndon and Dryhurst have called ‘identity play’: of farming content to increase, exaggerate and render irreducible your concept in the latent space. After all, the relational logic of social media, taken together with a min-maxed aesthetic of exaggeration and high variability seem to translate incredibly well to the farming of ‘cosine capital’ or ‘neural exchange value’ in the latent spaces of generative models. In this sense, as Mikael Brunila argues, what was once analysed as “algorithmic culture” is “undergoing a radical intensification” with the shift to embeddings. What was once central to cultural capital – and for that matter, venture capital – is transformed along the lines of a radical form of optimisation perhaps most saliently expressed by the broader -maxxing trend, which in turn is operationalised in the latent spaces of generative models.
